images.filename: Mobilizing equipment near the Fairbairn Water Treatment Plant (10601901265).jpg
images.caption: Crews for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District are mobilizing equipment in preparation for levee work this fall along the American River near the Fairbairn Water Treatment Plant in Sacramento, Calif., shown Oct. 3, 2013. The Corps built more than 20 miles of seepage cutoff walls into American River levees between 2000 and 2002, but work was set aside for later where complicated encroachments existed such as utilities, power lines and bridges. (U.S. Army photo by Todd Plain/Released)

images.filename: American River Bike Trail remains open near H Street Bridge during levee improvements (15701364787).jpg
images.caption: A cyclist on the American River Bike Trail heads toward the H Street Bridge in Sacramento, California Nov. 24, 2014. The trail will remain open throughout U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District levee improvement work on both sides of the bridge, scheduled to be completed in mid-2015. A special blend of cement, stored in the twin yellow tanks in the background, will be used to create a water-resistant wall in the levees. The Sacramento District built more than 20 miles of seepage cutoff walls into American River levees between 2000 and 2002, but set aside work around complicated encroachments until now. images.filename: Preparing for levee work near the Fairbairn Water Treatment Plant in Sacramento, Calif. (9577034279).jpg
images.caption: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District is preparing for levee work this summer along the American River near the Fairbairn Water Treatment Plant in Sacramento, Calif., shown Aug. 21, 2013. Water intake pipes, sewer mains and multiple utilities delayed levee construction near here more than a decade ago. The Army Corps built more than 20 miles of seepage cutoff walls into American River levees between 2000 and 2002, but work was set aside for later where complicated encroachments existed such as utilities, power lines and bridges. (U.S. Army photo by Todd Plain/Released)
images.alt: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District is preparing for levee work this summer along the American River near the Fairbairn Water Treatment Plant in Sacramento, Calif., shown Aug. 21, 2013. Water intake pipes, sewer mains and multiple utilities delayed levee construction near here more than a decade ago. The Army Corps built more than 20 miles of seepage cutoff walls into American River levees between 2000 and 2002, but work was set aside for later where complicated encroachments existed such as utilities, power lines and bridges. (U.S. Army photo by Todd Plain/Released)

images.filename: A view of the newly repaved American River Parkway trail (8201719300).jpg
images.caption: A view of the newly repaved American River Parkway trail near the California State University-Sacramento campus in Sacramento, Calif., shown Nov. 16, 2012. Construction representatives with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District inspected the remaining asphalt work as one of the last steps before the heavily-used recreational trail can reopen later this month. A detour was necessary while levee construction proceeded along the American River during the summer. The work is part of the American River Common Features project, a joint effort between the Corps, the state’s Central Valley Flood Protection Board and the Sacramento Area Flood Control Agency to reduce flood risk for Sacramento.  (U.S. Army photo by Todd Plain/Released)

images.filename: (R6) American River Bike Trail detour and levee construction map (7902578880).jpg
images.caption: A map of the American River’s north bank between Spanos Court and Campus Commons golf course in Sacramento, Calif., illustrates a bike trail detour during levee construction scheduled from August through November 2012. The map was included on informational fliers distributed to residents and published on the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District’s website in early July. The project is part of the American River Common Features program, a joint flood risk reduction effort between the Corps, the state’s Central Valley Flood Protection Board/Department of Water Resources and the Sacramento Area Flood Control Agency. (U.S. Army illustration/Released)

images.filename: Nov. 9, 2011 American River Parkway Trail near the California State University-Sacramento campus (6345164215).jpg
images.caption: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District finished a levee improvement project Oct. 31, 2011 along the American River Parkway Trail near the California State University-Sacramento campus, shown Nov. 9, 2011. Funded by the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009, the $2.2 million project installed a seepage cutoff wall in a 162-foot-long stretch of levee at the west end of Northrop Avenue. Construction on another levee improvement site nearby is scheduled to begin spring 2012. (U.S. Army photo by Todd Plain/RELEASED)
images.alt: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District finished a levee improvement project Oct. 31, 2011 along the American River Parkway Trail near the California State University-Sacramento campus, shown Nov. 9, 2011. Funded by the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009, the $2.2 million project installed a seepage cutoff wall in a 162-foot-long stretch of levee at the west end of Northrop Avenue.
